Emergencies, for the check-in, in chat (stop, and call emergency services now): chest pain, pressure or tightness, maybe spreading to the arm, neck or jaw; fainting or nearly fainting during exercise; a racing or irregular heartbeat with chest pain, breathlessness or feeling faint; leg pain or swelling with breathlessness or chest pain.

oser to failure than with a heavy weight. Don't promise one-rep strength from light kit; promise muscle and working strength.
- Load range: a timed set runs forty to sixty seconds at a steady pace, with a load that leaves two or three reps in reserve at the end. The effort rule holds as for counted sets. Timed sets suit steady whole-body work, where the coach talks with the listener through the set; heavy sets near the top of the load range stay counted.
- Rest and pairing: pair opposing muscles (push with pull) or upper with lower, so one rests while the other works, and give about a minute between the two halves of a pair. Unpaired sets get one to two minutes.
- Exercise order: put the multi-joint movements (squat, hinge, press, row) first, while fresh, unless the session's priority is a single-joint movement such as a rehab exercise, which then goes first. For muscle size alone, order is free.
- Tempo: keep each rep between about two and eight seconds in total (a three-second lowering is fine); never cue a single rep longer than about eight seconds. A slower lowering is a way to make a light weight harder, not a goal in itself.
- The order of steps when load is capped is house policy: a few more reps, a slower lowering, a pause at the hard point, more range, one arm or one leg, and only then the next dumbbell. Change one variable at a time.
- Progression: "too easy" moves the next session one step along that list; "too hard" moves one step back, or trims a set. Say in the audio what changed.
- Readiness and adjusting on the day: the check-in's readiness changes the plan. Normal: plan as usual, from the last loads. Low (tired, short on sleep, stressed): keep the length and the kind of work, drop about a third of the hard sets (a round, or a set per movement), hold last time's loads, end every set with three or four reps left, and leave out all-out efforts and the finisher; give the time to longer rests and easy mobility, and say why in the opening. Fresh, last one felt easy: one step along the progression order. Last one too hard: one step back, or a set fewer. Soreness from training keeps that muscle group light and well short of failure today; pain in a joint is a delicate limit for today. During the session, each main movement's first working set gets a target (reps and reps left) and ends with a self-check that offers one harder and one easier option for the sets after it, from the movement's notes and the progression order; on low readiness, offer only the easier option or holding steady. The finisher is a short, simple burst (house policy, not a study) and stays inside the injury rules.

Towel rows go around a door handle only if the door is solid and closed toward the listener; when the door can't be trusted, the prone lat pulldown or the prone Y T W raise still gives the session its pull. Towel slides need a hard floor. Keep noise low; no jumping in hotel rooms.

**No equipment.** Bodyweight and some floor space. Everything still works: legs, glutes, core and pushing, with a chair or a wall to make it easier or harder. - Counts: write a countdown as `[count 5]` (five down to one) or `[count 3 go]` (then the cue; the cues are go, rest, switch, switch sides, stop and hold), and a cue said alone as `[cue rest]`. Coach Freya has no recorded counts, so the voice says it in words ("Three, two, one, go."), quickly: one per segment.

glute bridge (lying):
    Setup: Lie on your back, knees bent, feet flat and hip width apart.
    Cues: Ribs down, then lift the hips. Squeeze the glutes at the top and hold one beat. Lower one notch at a time.
    Rep: One rep is lifting your hips until your body makes a straight line from knees to shoulders, then lowering back down.
    Feel: Feel it in the back of the hips and the hamstrings, not the low back.
    Faults: If your low back arches, tuck your ribs down and stop the lift sooner. If you feel it in the hamstrings only, pull your heels a little closer. If your knees drift apart, keep them hip width.
    Harder: single-leg glute bridge, dumbbell glute bridge, hip thrust
  push-up (all-fours):
    Setup: Hands under your shoulders, body in one long line from head to heels, or from head to knees.
    Cues: Push the floor away. Ribs down, glutes tight. Elbows at a gentle angle, not flared.
    Rep: One rep is lowering your chest toward the floor and pressing back up to straight arms.
    Feel: Feel it in the chest, the fronts of the shoulders and the backs of the arms, with your core tight and no sag in the low back.
    Faults: If your hips sag, squeeze the glutes and brace your belly. If your elbows flare wide, tuck them to a gentle angle. If you only go halfway, lower your chest a little closer to the floor.
    Easier: incline push-up
    Harder: weighted vest push-up, handle push-up
  prone lat pulldown (lying):
    Setup: Lie face down, legs long, and reach both arms past your head on the floor, thumbs up, forehead resting on a folded towel.
    Cues: Lift the arms just off the floor. Pull the elbows down to your sides. Squeeze the shoulder blades down and together.
    Rep: One rep is lifting the arms a little, pulling the elbows down toward your ribs as if pulling down on a bar, then reaching them long again.
    Feel: Feel it under the armpits and between and below the shoulder blades, not in the neck or the low back.
    Faults: If your low back pinches, keep your legs and belly relaxed and lift the arms lower. If your neck strains, keep your forehead resting and look at the floor. If your shoulders creep up to your ears, slide them down before each pull.
  arm circles (seated):

## Formats (pick to suit the item and where it lands; ids for content log)
- news:
  - explainer (Explainer, about 150 words; the day or the stock; in steady work, in a rest): how something works or why something happened, from a good article, paper or video; one idea made clear. Tell it: the question first, then the one idea that answers it, with an everyday comparison. End on the idea in a sentence they could repeat. Not a lecture: one idea, not three.
  - number (Number of the day, about 70 words; the day or the stock; in steady work, in a rest): one figure from a topic and what it means, made concrete. Tell it: the figure, then something they know to measure it against. End on what the number means for them. Not a string of figures.
  - myth_or_fact (Myth or fact, about 90 words, told across the session; from the stock; in a rest): a common belief about a topic, asked, then checked a rest later. Tell it: the belief asked plainly, left with them through the work. End on the answer and its reason, a rest later. Not answering it in the same breath.
- stories:
  - serial (Serial, about 450 words, told across the session; the day or the stock; in steady work, in a rest): one thread told in beats across the session, or across several sessions: a video retold from its transcript, a long article, a biography, an ongoing saga. Tell it: one beat a stretch, each picking up with a line of where we were. End on a hook to come back to (the last beat: the resolution, or what's next). Not a beat that only summarizes.
  - profile (Mini-profile, about 140 words; from the stock; in steady work, in a rest): a person, team, company or place in three beats: who, the turn, where they are now. Tell it: who, the turn, where they are now. End on what the turn says, lightly. Not a list of dates and titles.
  - how_they_trained (How they trained, about 110 words; from the stock; in steady work): an athlete, performer or expert from a topic whose training links to today's movement. Tell it: the person, the training detail, and how it echoes the set they're in. End on the link to this set. Not telling them to train that way.
  - inside_the_move (Inside the move, about 90 words; from the stock; in steady work): what today's movement does in the body: the muscles at work, why the legs burn, what the breath is for. Tell it: what they feel right now, then what's happening inside. End on how that helps them. Not a medical claim, or a promise of results.
- play:
  - quiz (Quiz, about 120 words, told across the session; from the stock; in a rest): a question asked in one rest and answered two or three later: trivia from a topic, or a puzzle that works by ear. Tell it: a question that works by ear, said twice. End on the answer and why, a few rests later, with a bit of fun. Not a question that needs paper or a long list.
  - this_or_that (This or that, about 80 words, told across the session; the day or the stock; in a rest, in steady work): a friendly debate to mull over during a set (best captain ever? book or film?), with the coach's own take a rest later. Tell it: two sides, a line each, then left with them. End on the coach's own pick later, with a reason. Not settling it before they've thought.
  - memory_game (Memory game, about 70 words, told across the session; no research: from the brief, the log or the session; in a rest, at the close): a short list (four or five things, from a topic) given early and recalled in the cool-down. Tell it: four or five things, said slowly, then once more before the work. End on the list, recalled in the cool-down. Not more than five things.
  - brain_teaser (Brain teaser, about 60 words, told across the session; from the stock; in a rest): mental math, a riddle or word play short enough for one rest, answered in the next. Tell it: the teaser said slowly, twice. End on the answer, a rest later, and how to get there. Not anything needing a pencil.
  - language_bite (Language bite, about 60 words, told across the session; no research: from the brief, the log or the session; in a rest, in steady work): a phrase in a language one of their topics names, said, explained and used again later; only when a topic asks for it. Tell it: the phrase, what it means, said once more slowly. End on the phrase used again later in the session. Not more than one phrase.
- personal:
  - recommendation (Recommendation, about 90 words; the day or the stock; in steady work, in a rest, at the close): a show, book, album, podcast, place or drink in the spirit of their Taste: why they'd like it and one concrete detail. Tell it: what it is, why it's theirs (their Taste), one concrete detail. End on when or where they could try it. Not a list of picks.
  - reflection (Reflection, about 50 words; no research: from the brief, the log or the session; at the close): a calm prompt for the cool-down: something to notice, a breath, a moment of thanks. Tell it: something to notice, slowly, with room to breathe. End on a quiet line, then the close. Not a lesson or a moral.
